summary: Cathedral City sits in the middle of the Coachella Valley floor, flanked by the San Jacinto Mountains to the west, which means winter sunsets regularly light up a 10,000-foot ridgeline visible from virtually any east-facing parking lot — a geological backdrop that would be a headline amenity anywhere else but here barely makes the brochure because Palm Springs, its immediate neighbor, absorbs most of the tourism attention. That adjacency matters economically: much of the employment base is tied to hospitality, healthcare, and retail serving the broader desert resort corridor, so switching jobs often means commuting along East Palm Canyon Drive or Interstate 10 rather than leaving the valley entirely. With a median home value around $420,700 against a median household income of roughly $67,000, the price-to-income ratio lands near 6.3× — more accessible than coastal California but still a stretch that pushes many households toward renting at around $1,554 per month. The climate is the defining daily fact: an annual average high of 83°F and 10.5 hours of sunshine per day mean summers are genuinely punishing (triple digits for months), while winters deliver the dry, warm days that justify the whole desert economy. The city's 22.7 square miles at roughly 2,300 people per square mile produce a spread-out, car-dependent layout — pockets of commercial strips separated by wide residential tracts and desert washes rather than a single walkable core. Cathedral City is, at bottom, a working desert city that happens to share a zip-code border with one of America's most famous resort towns, and the gap between those two identities shapes almost every tradeoff here.
